questions.question: What is the discrete logarithm problem in a group generated by g?
options: Given h = g^x, recover x modulo the order of g
Given x, compute h = g^x as quickly as possible
Given p, decide whether p is prime using repeated squaring
Given n, find two factors whose product equals n
questions.explanation: The DLP asks for the exponent x from h = g^x. Exponentiation is easy; recovering x should be hard in well-chosen groups.

questions.question: What does it mean for an integer to be smooth over a factor base?
options: It factors completely into the primes or elements in the chosen factor base
It is prime and smaller than every element in the factor base
It has no repeated prime factors after trial division
It is congruent to 1 modulo every factor-base element
questions.explanation: A smooth value has no leftover factor outside the base. That makes its logarithm a linear combination of factor-base logarithms.

questions.question: Why does a smooth relation g^k = 3^a * 5^b * 11^c produce a linear equation?
options: Taking logs base g gives k = a log_g(3) + b log_g(5) + c log_g(11) modulo the group order
Taking square roots gives k = a + b + c over the integers without a modulus
Applying Miller-Rabin gives a primality certificate for each factor-base element
Computing gcd(k, p) reveals the unknown exponent directly
questions.explanation: Discrete logs turn multiplication into addition and powers into scalar multiples, so smooth products become linear equations in unknown factor-base logs.

questions.question: Why does the lesson implement index calculus inside a prime-order subgroup?
options: Linear algebra modulo a prime order has invertible nonzero pivots, avoiding composite-modulus complications
Prime-order subgroups make every discrete log equal to zero, simplifying the attack
Index calculus only works in groups whose order is exactly two
Prime-order subgroups remove the need for a factor base
questions.explanation: The full group F_p* has order p-1, often composite. A prime-order subgroup lets the lesson use field linear algebra modulo q.

questions.question: What is the final descent step in index calculus?
options: Find t such that h*g^t is smooth, then subtract t from the smooth value's known log
Run trial division on p - 1 until the subgroup order is prime
Use Pollard rho to solve all factor-base logs one by one
Hash h into a new generator and restart relation collection
questions.explanation: Once factor-base logs are known, a shifted smooth target gives log(h) + t. Subtract t modulo the subgroup order to recover log(h).

questions.question: What makes index calculus a structural attack rather than a generic attack?
options: It uses the integer representation of finite-field elements and their factorization over small primes
It works only by observing timing differences in modular exponentiation
It ignores the group representation and treats multiplication as a black-box operation
It requires the target exponent to be reused in two different protocols
questions.explanation: Index calculus exploits smooth integer representatives in finite fields. Generic attacks like BSGS and Pollard rho do not use that representation.

questions.question: Why is shared finite-field parameter reuse relevant to index-calculus attacks?
options: Factor-base precomputation can be amortized across many targets in the same group
Reusing parameters makes p composite after enough public keys are generated
The generator changes order every time a new public key is published
All users automatically choose the same secret exponent
questions.explanation: The expensive relation collection and linear algebra depend on the group. Once done, many individual targets in that same group can be attacked more cheaply.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against custom small finite-field groups?
options: Index-calculus and small-subgroup issues can make discrete logs far easier than expected
Custom groups prevent modular exponentiation from being implemented at all
Small finite-field groups are secure only when the generator is even
Index calculus proves every finite-field group has polynomial-time discrete logs
questions.explanation: Small or poorly validated finite-field groups can be broken by structural DLP attacks and subgroup mistakes. Production systems should use vetted parameters and libraries.
